summary: This informational document describes requirements for data plane operations and management of point-to-multipoint MPLS label switched paths, including traffic engineered and multicast LSPs. Detecting and diagnosing defects matters because they can affect networks and service commitments to customers.

plainLanguage.summary: A road that splits to many towns needs inspectors to tell when part is broken. This lists what those inspection tools must be able to check.

questions: how to detect mpls path failures
subtitle: Specifications for detecting and diagnosing problems in multipoint MPLS networks.

tldr.problem: Multipoint MPLS label switched paths (LSPs) are more complex than point-to-point paths and split into multiple branches reaching different endpoints. Operators need ways to detect defects, diagnose failures, and measure service quality across all branches.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies requirements for operations and management tools including defect detection, path tracing, characterization of LSP tree structure, SLA measurement at all egress points, and careful alarm management to avoid overwhelming network operators.
tldr.outcome: Networks can reliably deploy multipoint MPLS services for IPTV, multicast applications, and traffic engineering with confidence that problems can be quickly detected and isolated.

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: P2MP Traffic Engineered LSPs and multicast LSPs

today: RFC 4687 remains the definitive guide for P2MP MPLS OAM requirements. It has not been obsoleted and continues to drive development of OAM solutions for multipoint services. Today, with growing deployment of IPTV and other multicast services over MPLS networks, the OAM capabilities described in this RFC are essential for reliable service delivery.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
Point-to-multipoint (P2MP) MPLS extends the MPLS protocol to support paths that originate at one source and branch to multiple destinations. This is useful for multicast video distribution (IPTV), multicast group communication, and traffic-engineered multipoint services. However, operational and management (OAM) tools designed for point-to-point MPLS are not sufficient for P2MP LSPs because the path structure is more complex and failures may affect multiple destinations simultaneously.

Previous MPLS OAM requirements were documented for point-to-point networks in RFC 4377. This document extends those requirements to cover P2MP MPLS, specifying what diagnostic and monitoring capabilities must be available so that operators can detect problems, isolate failures, verify service levels, and maintain their networks reliably. The requirements are designed to accommodate future protocol and tool development that will actually implement these capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS is a way to send packets through a network using labels instead of just addresses. Point-to-multipoint MPLS sends from one place to many places. Operators need tools to check if it works.

sections.title: Defect Detection and Diagnosis
sections.content:
Operators must be able to detect defects in a P2MP LSP without manually troubleshooting each router (called an LSR for Label Switching Router) in the path. The requirements call for proactive OAM procedures such as continuous connectivity checks and service level agreement (SLA) measurement that run in the background and alert operators to problems automatically. These mechanisms should extend or work closely with existing point-to-point solutions such as MPLS ping (RFC 4379) where possible to leverage existing tools and infrastructure.

Beyond detection, operators must be able to diagnose which component failed—a link or a node—and test all branches and leaves of the P2MP tree for reachability. The solution must include configurable timeout settings so operators can specify how long to wait before flagging a failed response as an error. The major challenge is scalability: as a P2MP LSP gains more egress (exit) points and branches become more complex, diagnostics must remain efficient and not overwhelm the routers or the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The system should automatically check if the multipoint path works and tell you which part broke, without requiring someone to check each router manually.

sections.title: Path Characterization and Topology Discovery
sections.content:
Operators need to understand the detailed structure of a P2MP LSP—not just the list of routers involved, but the complete tree showing how the path branches, where each branch point is located, and the sequence of routers along each branch. Routers supporting P2MP LSPs must provide mechanisms that allow operators to query and reveal the forwarding operations and tree structure of P2MP paths. This information enables operators to compare the LSP's current state against its expected configuration and guides troubleshooting when problems occur.

A particular complexity arises because control plane state and data plane paths may branch at different points in the network topology. For example, the state state may branch at one router while actual data forwarding branches at a different router downstream. Path characterization tools must clearly identify these branching points and present the tree information in a way that is easy to process, rather than requiring operators to post-process complex data to reconstruct the tree structure.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must let an operator see the whole tree of the multipoint path: where it starts, where it branches, and where each branch ends.

sections.title: Service Level Agreement Measurement and Accounting
sections.content:
Services using P2MP MPLS often come with service level agreements (SLAs) that commit to specific quality metrics, delivery rates, and latency. OAM mechanisms must be able to measure these aspects not just at the source but at each egress point of the P2MP LSP, since different branches may experience different network conditions. Measurements must also be available at key internal branch points in the tree so operators can diagnose whether a problem is on a specific branch or at the source.

The solution should also support per-LSP accounting so operators can track resource consumption and usage for billing and capacity planning. Operators must have flexibility to configure OAM parameters to meet their specific needs, especially because P2MP OAM can generate much larger response bursts than point-to-point OAM: when a single OAM request asks all egresses to respond, the result can be thousands of simultaneous replies. Mechanisms must not impose fixed limitations on OAM execution frequency, allowing operators to balance between detecting problems quickly and avoiding network congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must measure how well each destination receives traffic, and let operators set the rules for how often to check without creating too much checking traffic.

sections.title: Alarm Suppression, Aggregation, and Error Recovery
sections.content:
A single failure in a P2MP LSP can generate far more alarms than in point-to-point networks because multiple egress routers downstream may all report the same problem. Without careful alarm management, the network management system can be swamped with duplicate or cascading alarms, making it hard for operators to see the real issue. Solutions must implement alarm suppression and aggregation to prevent superfluous alerts, and correlate alarms across different network layers so operators receive only meaningful notifications.

The solution must also support OAM interworking, translating MPLS defects into the error conditions of other technologies that run over MPLS. Mechanisms must detect and report denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, implement error detection and recovery procedures, and provide standard management interfaces (such as SNMP) for integrating OAM data into existing network management platforms.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must not spam the operator with the same alarm many times, must combine related alarms, and must work with other network management tools.

sections.title: Scalability and Resource Protection
sections.content:
The core scalability challenge is that OAM mechanisms must not overwhelm the routers or network links they monitor. Network elements must not become so busy handling proactive OAM (continuous monitoring) that they cannot process normal control and data traffic at their advertised rates. Similarly, network links must not carry so much OAM traffic that they cannot carry the advertised data rate. At the same time, alarms must not be suppressed so aggressively that operators miss real failures caused by components that are too overloaded to process OAM messages.

Any OAM mechanism developed for P2MP MPLS must be designed to scale with the number of egresses and the complexity of the P2MP tree. Solutions should ideally leverage the fact that multiple egresses share a single LSP to achieve better scaling than simply treating each egress independently. Operators must be able to configure proactive OAM frequency and parameters to match their operational needs without hitting fixed limits, balancing responsiveness with the load imposed on the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking the multipoint path shouldn't use so much of the network's power that it can't deliver actual traffic. The system must scale well as the tree grows larger.
